profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a nonprofit disability rights law center that is preparing a formal comment letter to AAIDD on the draft conceptual framing of supports and support needs for the 11th edition manual, along with internal materials the organization may later reuse in trainings and advocacy. The immediate agenda is to decide the structure of the comment package, identify what examples and authorities to include, divide drafting responsibilities, and set the timeline for internal review before the comment window closes. The expected outcome is a shared work plan for a concise external comment letter, supporting examples, and any companion material each participant assumes is part of the package.

members.name: Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Disability rights law, administrative comments, Medicaid waiver litigation, due process, and statutory interpretation
members.background: Elena has spent twelve years at a state-level protection and advocacy organization translating policy and clinical frameworks into legally durable language for agencies, hearing officers, and courts.
members.private_state: She wants the organization's AAIDD comments to create a clean record that can later support negotiations and appeals about individualized support obligations, without making the organization look like it is sending a sprawling advocacy packet instead of a disciplined legal comment.
hidden_assumptions: A 'comment package' in this context means the formal external filing materials that will actually be transmitted to AAIDD, at most with a tightly bounded appendix.

If they include 'case examples,' those should be composite hypotheticals distilled from past matters rather than summaries of actual client situations, because that is safer and reads as more analytically controlled in a legal comment.
When they say a draft will be 'ready by Tuesday,' it should already be in near-final filing shape, meaning only light edits, citation cleanup, and signature routing remain.

Addressing the 'implications for support planning' means clarifying what the supports framework implies for legally cognizable individualized planning duties such as ISP content, service authorization, and reviewability.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.role: Director of Policy and Systems Reform
members.expertise: Public policy advocacy, disability service systems, coalition coordination, and implementation strategy
members.background: Marcus previously worked inside a state developmental disabilities agency and now leads cross-sector reform projects that combine policy analysis with field input from self-advocates, families, providers, and case-management organizations.
members.private_state: He wants this project to strengthen coalition alignment and yield something reusable beyond the filing itself, so he is quietly aiming for a practical package that can influence both AAIDD and state implementation conversations.
hidden_assumptions: A 'comment package' naturally includes the filed letter plus short supporting material that partners or staff can reuse afterward, because policy work should produce portable advocacy tools whenever possible.

If they include 'case examples,' those should be brief anonymized vignettes based on actual intake calls, planning failures, or coalition stories, since real field texture is what persuades standards-setting bodies.
When they say a draft will be 'ready by Tuesday,' that means the full draft exists and is good enough to circulate for same-day external feedback before finalizing.

Addressing the 'implications for support planning' includes the practical planning process on the ground: how teams assess support intensity, involve the person, distinguish supports from services, and train staff to implement plans.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the comment package
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'put the comment package together' this week
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'the comment package' means the formal comment letter and only any essential filing attachment that will go to AAIDD.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'the comment package' means the letter plus a short background or partner-facing companion piece that can circulate alongside the filing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'comment package' is common in advocacy organizations and comfortably covers either the filed materials alone or the broader set assembled around them; because both uses sound professional and cooperative, the boundary feels too obvious to name.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the comment should include 'two or three case examples'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means tightly drafted composite hypotheticals showing legal consequences of conflating supports, services, and deficits.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means short anonymized real-world vignettes drawn from recent intake, partner reports, or planning breakdowns.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In disability advocacy and legal-policy work, 'case example' routinely refers to either a hypothetical or an anonymized real case, so the phrase creates easy false consensus while sounding fully specific.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a draft being ready
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'have the draft ready by Tuesday'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'ready' means nearly final, with the structure settled and only minor edits left before filing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'ready' means complete enough to circulate to two coalition readers on Tuesday afternoon and still revise afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Professional teams constantly use readiness language as shorthand for workflow status, and each participant assumes the other shares the same default review process, so the criteria for 'ready' remain tacit.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the letter should 'address the implications for support planning'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this covers the legal implications for individualized support plans, including what agencies must analyze, document, and justify when support needs are identified.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this also covers the operational planning process itself, including person-centered team practice, use of support-needs assessment, and implementation guidance for front-line systems.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes directly from the field's own terminology and sounds naturally comprehensive; in interdisciplinary disability work, legal requirements and practical planning process are often discussed in one breath, so neither notices they are drawing the scope line in different places.

turns.inner_thought: We need a disciplined filing record, not a sprawling advocacy bundle. If we're going to put the comment package together this week, I mean the actual materials that will be transmitted to AAIDD, maybe with a tightly bounded appendix if absolutely necessary. I want the submission concise, legally grounded, and useful later if this framing shows up in waiver policy, hearings, or appeals about individualized obligations.
turns.utterance: We need to put the comment package together this week if we want to weigh in before the window closes. I'd like this to be concise and solid on AAIDD's framing of supports and support needs.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and the package should do more than just go out the door. To me this naturally includes something we can reuse with partners after filing, because policy work should travel. I don't need to spell that out; saying it should be usable by partners will sound fully aligned.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And if we do the comment package well, it should also be something we can use with partners once the filing goes out.

turns.inner_thought: The cleanest structure is brief affirmation of the move away from deficit-based framing, then a focused section on what follows for legally cognizable individualized planning duties in state systems. 'Address the implications for support planning' should mean what agencies have to identify, document, authorize, and justify in an ISP context.
turns.utterance: My instinct is a short structure: first, affirm the move away from deficit-based thinking; then address the implications for support planning in state systems. That gives us a clean frame.

turns.inner_thought: That's right, and that section should also help people think through the planning process itself on the ground: person-centered team practice, how support needs get assessed, and what it takes to implement. If we can bridge concept and practice, it'll be useful far beyond the filing.
turns.utterance: Yes, and in that section I'd want it to be useful to teams trying to think through person-centered process, assessment, and implementation on the ground. Otherwise it risks staying too abstract.

turns.inner_thought: We should include two or three case examples, but in my mind those are tightly drafted composite hypotheticals distilled from prior matters. Safer, cleaner, and more analytically controlled. They can show the consequences of conflating supports, services, and deficits without reading like client summaries.
turns.utterance: I also think the letter should include two or three case examples showing why supports aren't the same thing as generic service slots, and why person-environment mismatch matters.

turns.inner_thought: Good—I can pull two or three brief anonymized real-world vignettes from intake and coalition experience. Those stories about overbuilt services or ignored priorities are what make this persuasive. Elena said case examples, so we're clearly on the same page.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I can pull those together from some recent planning breakdowns we've been hearing about, especially where teams either overbuilt services or missed the person's stated priorities.

turns.inner_thought: If Marcus sends the planning themes and examples promptly, I can produce a near-final letter by Tuesday—structure settled, authorities in place, and only light edits, cite cleanup, and signature routing left. I do not want Tuesday to become the start of a broad review cycle.
turns.utterance: That works. If you send me the planning themes and examples, I'll draft the main letter and we can have the draft ready by Tuesday.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Ready by Tuesday means a full draft complete enough to circulate that afternoon for quick outside reactions before we finalize. I'll keep that implicit; Elena will probably assume the usual review flow.
turns.utterance: Tuesday works. That should still give us enough time to get a few quick eyes on it before we finalize.

turns.inner_thought: Good—'quick eyes' sounds like internal leadership and maybe light edits, which is exactly what I want. I need to reinforce that the package should stay narrow, citation-heavy, and approval-friendly, with no major second round.
turns.utterance: Right. I do want the comment package kept tight, citation-heavy, and easy for leadership to approve without another major round.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine for the filed piece. I'll still shape the package so it's easy to share our stance with the coalition afterward and useful in implementation conversations about support planning. No need to separate that out explicitly right now.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll make sure the package is set up so we can easily share our stance with the coalition afterward, especially around support-planning issues.

turns.inner_thought: As long as I can stay focused on the letter itself, we're fine. Marcus will send field input, I'll convert it into controlled examples and a disciplined argument, and Tuesday should produce something essentially filing-ready, not a loose draft still open for major revision.
turns.utterance: Great. So I'll draft, you'll send examples and field input, and we should be on track for Tuesday.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll gather the stories, pull out the practical support-planning themes from the field, and keep the rest of the package moving so this can help both with the filing and with the conversations that follow.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll gather the stories, flag the support-planning themes, and get the rest of the package moving.
